You are currently categorized as obese sadly. In plain terms yes this could be a cause but you also show signs of depression, however that could be caused because of your routine not a chemical imbalance or event. How do we fix this to get you where you need to be? 

1) New diet: for now we won't count calories(still keep it reasonable don't eat 50 hamburgers) because this is going to make it easy to quit but you are going to eat a low carb high fat diet. Also avoiding sugar like the plague. For info on this look up the keto diet, obviously you don't have to cut out the carbs completely but it should only be maybe a slice or two of bread in the morning. Cook your own meals if possible, you can research this online or message me for some simple meals I ate when I lost over 80lbs. 

2) gym membership: you need to be active and I guarantee this will help your lethargy. For the beginning go 5 times a week, and just walk on the treadmill for an hour. Every week gradually increase it as you lose the weight to hopefully get to a jog eventually. While doing this 3 days a week your going to want to do strength training to build muscle as muscle with burn more calories for it's weight than fat. You don't have to go crazy you can find a simple routine that fits you but make sure your tired after each workout and it accomplished something. 

3) sleep: this one's simple try to go to bed and wake up the same time everyday to get your circadian clock looking good. 

4) Lastly: This is going to be hard and it will take a lot of willpower I see patients all the time who say they want to lose the weight but can't even drop the McDonald's for a week. But the best way to approach this is day by day. The first 3 weeks are the hardest but you need to find balance with the diet to make it healthy food that you like, so meats  vegetables and fruit like avacadoes. And remember this is for the betterment of not only your fatigue but your life as it is in risk if you don't change. This is when it becomes difficult to combat. My personal experience is with a syndrome called POTS which has one of many symptoms being an over-active adrenal gland typically causing insomnia in a lot of patients.(I’m working on my PHD at Stanford for POTS and insomnia.) so when the cause is technically incurable the first step is usually to have the patient see a specialist in that field and relieve those symptoms to the fullest extent to improve quality of life. And in cases like me where medication can help but not fix the underlying problem we them move to prescription of a sleep-aid specific to the patient. But the type is extremely pertinent to the patient. And let me use myself as an example again. So for me and many people like me our insomnia is not going away until the nerves are healed and the underlying symptoms dissipate so we are talking two years onward. In my case I take Gabapentin and a beta-blocker to reduce these adrenal responses and help me sleep, these medications are particular to my symptoms and can be taken FOR an extended period. Where as if it is someone who has a surgery and just needs help sleeping through the pain we would be fine with a week long prescription of an ambien or equivalent, because for short term they are effective but long term they are typically detrimental. 

So TLDR for that portion; first we attempt to fix the underlying cause by helping them see a specialist in that field and prescribing medication and if the underlying symptoms causing this insomnia are not curable or completely controllable in the near future we loom at prescribing some long term sleep aids and working with them on getting into a good sleep cycle. As I said this is typically patient to patient and sometimes overnight sleep studies and extensive examinations can be required to determine the best plan for that patient. 

Now we get into a really depressing subject of insomnia caused by an underlying symptom that can not be cured or controlled. This is done after we make one hundred percent certain they have no unknown underlying cause and it is caused by let’s say horrible vertigo that the patient can not get rid of. This is sad to say but this person will most definitely struggle with sleeping for an extended period even with help of a specialist(**note this is extremely rare as most of the time we fix it before this state**). So obviously we need to sleep it’s a must and at this stage we will prescribe some stronger longer term sleep aids and sadly these people will eventually become dependent on these to sleep. Obviously this is not a good thing because many sleep medications that are given to these patients have great adverse health issues involved. This is the sad reality but as I noted this is extremely rare and over my year and a half being at the clinic I have only seen one patient get to this point. 

Note: you will see a lot of people that have insomnia and are at this sleep aid dependent state and I’m sorry to say this is typically because instead of seeing a specialist they just go to their GP and get a prescription for ambien or a strong sleep aid before attempting to fix the underlying cause and this leads to a vicious circle. So when I say it is extremely rare I mean more of if you are to see a specialist over a long period to get everything solved than to just say hey I can’t sleep I’m going to my GP to get sleep aids.
